intro: People all over the world keep old stories. Grandparents tell them. Children learn them. Then the children tell them again.
In this unit you will hear stories from many groups. You will see special books and how people care for them. You will learn to say, "This is a story that ___ tell."
bigQuestion: Why do people keep stories and books safe for so long?

timeline.t: Grandpa tells Leo an old story
We hear the story of Noah and the ark
We hear about the prince who looked outside
We hear how lamps welcomed Rama home
We hear how Guru Nanak shared food
The librarian opens the glass case
We learn how people hold their holy books
We tell a story to a friend

words.d: a way a group of people believe, pray and live together
being kind and careful with what matters to someone else
the very big boat Noah builds in the story
a man who lives simply and spends his life on his religion
a Hindu festival of lights in the fall
a free meal Sikhs share with anyone who comes
a long sheet rolled up, not cut into pages
to say words out loud, often from memory

test.q: Who tells the story of Noah?
test.why: The Bible and Qur'an tell of Noah.

test.q: Who tells the story of Prince Siddhartha?
test.why: This is a story Buddhists tell.

test.q: What did Guru Nanak do with the money?
test.why: Sikhs call this the true trade.

test.q: Which holy book is a scroll?
test.why: The Torah rolls on two poles.
The Qur'an is the holy book of Islam.

test.q: Where do people keep holy books?
test.why: People keep them off the floor.

choices: To say words aloud from memory

test.q: What is a kind way to share a story?
choices: "This is a story that Hindus tell."
test.why: Naming who tells it is kind and true.

write.prompt: Pick one story or book from this unit. Draw it. Then say or write: "This is a story (or book) that ___ keep." Tell one way people care for it or one thing it helps them remember.
tips: Name the group: Jews, Christians, Muslims, Hindus, Buddhists or Sikhs.
Use one word from the unit, like scroll or langar.
Tell what people do, not what is best.

title: Stories People Keep

chapters.title: Old Stories from Many Lands
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do people keep telling the same old stories?

story.title: A Story from Grandpa
story.kicker: Grandpa has a story that is older than anyone he knows.
paragraphs: It is a rainy Saturday. Leo sits on the rug. Grandpa sits in his big chair. He pats the seat next to him. Leo hops up fast. Leo hops up.
"Sit down," Grandpa says. "This is a story my grandpa told me. His grandpa told it to him. It is very, very old. Now I will tell it to you."
Leo leans close. The rain taps on the window. Grandpa's voice gets soft and slow. Leo listens to every single word. He does not want to miss any of it.
When the story ends, Leo asks, "Can I tell it to my friend Sam?" Grandpa smiles. "Yes. That is how old stories stay alive."
story.think: Who tells you stories at home or at school? Is there one you like to hear again?

lessons.title: A Story Told Again
lessons.mainIdea: Some stories are told again and again for a very long time.
reading: A family can keep a story. So can a big group of people. They tell it to children. The children grow up and tell it too.
Some of these stories come from religions. A *religion* is a way people believe and live together. Each group keeps its own stories.

words.d: a way a group of people believe, pray and live together

look.title: A Story Chain
look.text: Picture five people in a line. Great-grandma tells a story to Grandma. Grandma tells Mom. Mom tells Leo. Leo tells baby June.
look.prompt: How many people heard the same story? Who will June tell it to?

check.q: What is an old story?
choices: A story told for a very long time
A story made up this morning
check.why: Old stories are passed from one person to the next for many years.

check.q: Who told Leo's grandpa the story?
check.why: Grandpa said his grandpa told him the story.

check.q: What is a religion?
choices: A way a group believes and lives together
check.why: A religion is a way people believe, pray and live together.

lessons.title: Saying Whose Story It Is
lessons.mainIdea: We say which group tells a story.
reading: We can say, "This is a story that Hindus tell." Or, "This is a story that Sikhs tell." Those words tell us whose story it is.
Saying it this way is kind and true. It shows respect. It helps us learn about our friends and neighbors.

words.d: being kind and careful with what matters to someone else

look.title: Fill the Blank
look.text: Mia hears a story about a boat. Her teacher says Jews, Christians and Muslims tell it. Mia starts to share: "This is a story that ___ tell."
look.prompt: What words can Mia put in the blank?

check.q: Which words tell whose story it is?
choices: "This is a story that Sikhs tell."
check.why: Naming the group tells whose story it is, kindly.

check.q: Why do we say which group tells a story?
check.why: Saying who tells a story is true and shows respect.

check.q: What does respect mean?
choices: Being kind and careful with what matters to others
check.why: Respect means being careful with what matters to someone else.

lessons.title: Noah and the Big Boat
lessons.mainIdea: Jews, Christians and Muslims all tell a story about Noah.
reading: In the story, a great flood comes. Noah builds a big boat called an *ark*. He brings his family and many animals inside.
Jews and Christians read this story in the Bible. Muslims read about Noah, called Nuh, in the Qur'an. In the Bible, a rainbow comes at the end.

words.d: the very big boat Noah builds in the story
a lot of water that covers the land

look.title: From the Book of Genesis
look.text: And the bow shall be in the cloud; and I will look upon it, that I may remember the everlasting covenant between God and every living creature.
look.prompt: In the story, what is in the cloud? What does it help people remember?

check.q: What does Noah build?
choices: A big boat called an ark
check.why: In the story, Noah builds an ark.

check.q: Which groups tell a story about Noah?
check.why: Jews, Christians and Muslims all tell of Noah.

check.q: In the Bible story, what comes at the end?
check.why: Genesis tells of a bow, or rainbow, in the cloud.

lessons.title: The Prince Who Looked Outside
lessons.mainIdea: Buddhists tell of a prince who saw that people grow old and get sick.
reading: Buddhists tell of a prince named Siddhartha. He lived in a palace long ago. He did not know about sadness.
One day he rode outside. He saw an old man and a sick man. Then he saw a *monk*, a man who lived simply. Buddhists say he later became the Buddha.

words.d: a man who lives simply and spends his life on his religion
a name that means "the one who woke up"

look.title: What the Prince Saw
look.text: The prince rides past the palace wall. First he sees an old man with a cane. Next a sick man in bed. Then a calm monk walking.
look.prompt: How do you think the prince felt? What might he want to find out?

check.q: Who tells the story of the prince Siddhartha?
check.why: This is a story that Buddhists tell.

check.q: Who did the prince see last?
check.why: In the story, he saw an old man, a sick man, then a monk.

check.q: What does the name Buddha mean?
check.why: Buddha means "the one who woke up."

lessons.title: Lamps for Rama
lessons.mainIdea: Hindus tell how lamps welcomed Rama home.
reading: Hindus tell a story about Prince Rama. He was sent far away. He stayed away for fourteen years.
At last, Rama came home. The people lit rows of little lamps. Many Hindus remember this at *Diwali*, the festival of lights.

words.d: a Hindu festival of lights in the fall
a small light; for Diwali, often a clay cup with oil

look.title: A Row of Lights
look.text: Picture a dark night. Tiny clay lamps sit on every step. Each one has a little flame. A family waits at the door.
look.prompt: Why might people light lamps for someone coming home?

check.q: What did the people light when Rama came home?
check.why: In the story, people lit rows of lamps.

check.q: Which festival remembers Rama's return?
check.why: Many Hindus remember Rama's return at Diwali.

check.q: Who tells the story of Rama?
check.why: This is a story that Hindus tell.

lessons.title: Guru Nanak Shares Food
lessons.mainIdea: Sikhs tell how Guru Nanak shared food with people who were hungry.
reading: Sikhs tell a story about young Guru Nanak. His father gave him money. "Make a good trade," his father said.
Nanak met hungry people. He used the money to buy them food. Sikhs call this the true trade. Today Sikhs share free meals called *langar*.

words.d: a teacher; Sikhs have ten human Gurus
a free meal Sikhs share with anyone who comes

look.title: A Sikh Teaching
look.text: Those who work hard for what they eat, and share some of what they have, know the true way.
look.cite: Guru Granth Sahib, p. 1245 (Guru Nanak), in plain words
look.prompt: What two things does this teaching ask people to do?

check.q: What did Guru Nanak buy with the money?
check.why: In the story, he fed hungry people.

check.q: What is langar?
check.why: Langar is a free shared meal at a Sikh gurdwara.

check.q: Who tells the story of Guru Nanak?
check.why: This is a story that Sikhs tell.

review.q: Who tells the story of Noah?
review.why: The Bible and the Qur'an both tell of Noah.

choices: The prince who saw an old man

review.q: What do many Hindus remember at Diwali?
What do Sikhs share at langar?
review.why: Langar is a free shared meal.

review.q: Which words say whose story it is?
choices: "This is a story that Hindus tell."
review.why: Naming the group is kind and true.

review.q: How do old stories stay alive?
choices: People tell them again and again
review.why: Stories live when each person tells the next.

chapters.title: Books People Keep Safe
chapters.bigQuestion: How do people show that a book is special to them?

story.title: The Glass Case
story.kicker: The librarian has four books that never touch the floor.
paragraphs: Ms. Ortiz is the school librarian. Today she walks to a glass case. The class follows her very quietly. Everyone wants to see.
Inside are four books. "People care for these books in special ways," she says. "Their families never leave them on the floor."
One is a scroll on two wooden rollers. One is wrapped in soft cloth. One sits on a little stand. One is a big book with a gold cover.
"Can we touch them?" asks Amir. Ms. Ortiz smiles. "First, let us learn how people hold them. Then we will use our careful hands."
story.think: Do you have a book or a thing that you keep extra safe? How do you care for it?

lessons.title: Four Special Books
lessons.mainIdea: Many religions have a book that they keep with great care.
reading: Jews read the *Torah*. Christians read the Bible. Muslims read the Qur'an. Sikhs read the Guru Granth Sahib.
Each book is special to its people. Other people can find it interesting. We can learn about all of them.

words.d: the first five books of the Hebrew Bible, special to Jews
the holy book of Islam, special to Muslims

look.title: Match the Book
look.text: Four friends each bring a picture. Ruth brings a Torah scroll. Luke brings a Bible. Aisha brings a Qur'an. Jas brings the Guru Granth Sahib.
look.prompt: Which friend's picture shows the book Sikhs read? Which shows the book Muslims read?

check.q: Which book do Muslims read?
check.why: The Qur'an is the holy book of Islam.

check.q: Which book do Sikhs read?
check.why: Sikhs read the Guru Granth Sahib.

check.q: Which book do Jews read?
check.why: The Torah is special to Jews.

lessons.title: A Scroll and a Book
lessons.mainIdea: A Torah is a long scroll; the others are books with pages.
reading: A *scroll* is one long rolled paper. The Torah scroll rolls on two wooden poles. Someone writes it all by hand.
The Bible, the Qur'an and the Guru Granth Sahib are books with pages. People turn the pages instead of rolling.

words.d: a long sheet rolled up, not cut into pages

look.title: Roll or Turn?
look.text: Picture two things on a table. One is rolled up tight on two poles. One has a cover and many flat pages.
look.prompt: Which one is a scroll? How would you open each one?

check.q: What is a scroll?
choices: One long sheet that is rolled up
check.why: A scroll is rolled, not cut into pages.

check.q: How is a Torah scroll written?
check.why: A Torah scroll is written all by hand.

check.q: Which one is a book with pages?
check.why: The Qur'an is a book with pages.

lessons.title: Clean Hands and Covers
lessons.mainIdea: People wash, cover and hold their holy books with care.
reading: Many Muslims wash before they touch the Qur'an. They may keep it on a stand. They keep it wrapped or up high.
The Torah scroll wears a cloth cover. Readers use a pointer called a *yad* so fingers do not touch the words.

words.d: a small pointer used to follow the words in a Torah scroll
a cloth that keeps a holy book safe

look.title: Getting Ready to Read
look.text: A girl washes her hands. She sets her Qur'an on a wooden stand. Her big brother points along a Torah scroll with a silver yad.
look.prompt: What careful things do you see? Why might people do them?

check.q: What is a yad?
choices: A pointer for reading the Torah
check.why: A yad lets readers follow words without touching them.

check.q: What do many Muslims do before touching the Qur'an?
check.why: Many Muslims wash before holding the Qur'an.

check.q: What does the Torah scroll wear?
check.why: The Torah scroll is dressed in a cloth cover.

lessons.title: Kept High and Safe
lessons.mainIdea: People keep holy books up high, never on the floor.
reading: In a gurdwara, the Guru Granth Sahib sits up high. It rests under a cloth *canopy*. At night it goes to its own room.
In a synagogue, the Torah scrolls rest in a cabinet called the ark. Many Christians keep a big Bible on a stand.

words.d: a cloth roof held up over something special
a Sikh place of worship

look.title: Where Does It Go?
look.text: Amir finds a Bible on the library floor. He remembers what Ms. Ortiz said. He picks it up gently.
look.prompt: Where might Amir put the book? Why?

check.q: Where does the Guru Granth Sahib sit in a gurdwara?
check.why: It rests up high under a cloth canopy.

check.q: Where do Torah scrolls rest in a synagogue?
choices: Under a canopy in a gurdwara
In a cabinet called the ark
check.why: Torah scrolls rest in the ark.

check.q: What is a gurdwara?
check.why: A gurdwara is where Sikhs gather.

lessons.title: Words Out Loud
lessons.mainIdea: People read and sing their holy books out loud.
reading: Many Muslims learn to *recite* the Qur'an in Arabic. To recite is to say words from memory, often like a song.
In a synagogue, the Torah is chanted. Sikhs sing hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib. Christians read the Bible aloud in church.

words.d: to say words out loud, often from memory

look.title: From the Book of Deuteronomy
look.text: And these words, which I command thee this day, shall be in thine heart: And thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children.
look.prompt: Who does this passage say should learn the words?

check.q: What does recite mean?
choices: To say words out loud from memory
check.why: To recite is to say words aloud, often from memory.

check.q: How do Sikhs share the Guru Granth Sahib?
check.why: Sikhs sing hymns from the Guru Granth Sahib.

check.q: In the Deuteronomy passage, who should be taught?
check.why: The verse says to teach the words to children.

lessons.title: Special to Some, Open to All
lessons.mainIdea: A book can be special to one family and still interesting to everyone.
reading: A holy book may be very special to one family. Another family may not read it at home. Some families have no holy book.
Every family is welcome in the *library*. The library keeps copies of many books. Anyone can learn about them.

words.d: a place that keeps books for everyone to read and learn from

look.title: Two Friends, Two Books
look.text: Sam's family reads the Bible at dinner. Priya's family reads no holy book. At the library, both look at the Guru Granth Sahib together.
look.prompt: What can Sam and Priya learn together?

check.q: Who can learn about a holy book?
check.why: Anyone can learn about any book at the library.

check.q: What does the school library keep?
check.why: The library keeps copies for everyone.

check.q: Does every family read a holy book?
check.why: Some families have no holy book, and that is fine.

review.why: The Torah is a scroll on two wooden poles.

review.q: What is a yad used for?
choices: Pointing to the words in a Torah
review.why: Readers use a yad to follow the words.

review.q: Where does the Guru Granth Sahib rest?
choices: In a cabinet called the ark
review.why: In a gurdwara it rests under a canopy.

review.q: What do many Muslims do before holding the Qur'an?
Where do holy books never go?
review.why: People keep holy books off the floor.
